entry.title: US Judge Acquits MIT-Educated Brothers in $25 Million Ethereum Heist Case
entry.content:
Links: reuters.com

A U.S. federal judge ordered the acquittal of two MIT-educated brothers who faced criminal charges for allegedly executing a $25 million cryptocurrency heist in 12 seconds. The case centered on an advanced exploit of Ethereum's validator system, with prosecutors arguing the brothers manipulated blockchain mechanics. However, the court determined that the government did not establish the necessary material misrepresentations required to support the fraud convictions.

entry.title: US Department of Commerce Implements New Export Controls on Remote AI Compute Access
entry.content:

The U.S. Commerce Department has introduced interim export controls requiring licenses for transferring advanced AI chips and servers to international data centers that could supply computing power to restricted countries, including China. The rules aim to close loopholes that allowed companies in embargoed nations to bypass direct shipping restrictions by utilizing foreign remote infrastructure.

The regulations apply to data networks exceeding 12 million total processing performance and mandate heightened customer vetting by exporters and data center operators. In addition, the framework imposes new licensing requirements for advanced semiconductor transfers to several countries identified as having high diversion risks, while formally rescinding the Biden administration's previous AI Diffusion Rule.

entry.title: Jakub T. Jankiewicz Argues All AI-Generated Code Should Be Open Source
entry.content:
Links: jakub.jankiewicz.org | hacker news

Software developer Jakub T. Jankiewicz argues that all code generated by artificial intelligence should be released as open source. He contends that because AI models are trained on scraped open-source repositories and crowd-sourced platforms like Stack Overflow without proper attribution, withholding the resulting output as proprietary software amounts to license laundering.

Jankiewicz also points to legal precedents, noting that purely AI-generated works lack human authorship and therefore generally cannot be copyrighted, as established by digital copyright disputes and policies such as Wikimedia Commons' public domain tagging for AI media. He suggests that releasing AI-assisted code under open-source licenses or Creative Commons Zero addresses international legal discrepancies and honors the collaborative foundations of modern software development.

entry.title: Judge Denies Dismissal of DRAM Supply Conspiracy Suit Against Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron
entry.content:
Links: litnews.ai | hacker news

A U.S. federal judge denied a joint motion by Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron to dismiss a proposed class action accusing the memory manufacturers of conspiring to restrict conventional DRAM supplies. The lawsuit alleges the companies intentionally choked off production of standard memory chips like DDR5 to shift manufacturing capacity toward high bandwidth memory.

U.S. District Judge Noël Wise ruled that the plaintiffs plausibly alleged an antitrust conspiracy under the Sherman Act, citing plus factors such as long-term HBM lock-ups, refusals to enter long-term conventional DRAM contracts, plant construction delays, and near-identical customer-vetting practices. The court ordered defendants to answer the complaint by December 7, 2026, and scheduled an initial case management conference for January 12, 2027.

entry.title: Electronic Frontier Foundation and ACLU Ask Appeals Court to Require Warrant for ALPR Searches
entry.content:
Links: eff.org | hacker news

The Electronic Frontier Foundation and the ACLU have filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, arguing that law enforcement searches of automated license plate reader (ALPR) databases constitute a "search" under the Fourth Amendment. The brief contends that mass ALPR tracking gives police a virtual time machine into individuals' past movements and should require a warrant.

The case stems from a series of robberies in Ohio where police identified a suspect's vehicle by running open-ended searches in Flock and ELSAG ALPR databases without a warrant. A lower court previously ruled that the defendant had no reasonable expectation of privacy regarding his license plate number in public, a finding that civil liberties groups are urging the appeals court to overturn.

entry.title: Electronic Frontier Foundation Warns Wearable Recording Devices Threaten Bystander Privacy
entry.content:
Links: eff.org | hacker news

The proliferation of ambient surveillance wearables—including smart glasses from Meta and Google, transcription-enabled watches from Apple, and recording hardware from Amazon—is shifting the concept of privacy away from individual choice toward unavoidable background monitoring. These devices capture continuous audio, video, or data throughout the day, effectively implicating everyone in a user's vicinity regardless of their consent.

While technology companies offer various technical safeguards and privacy controls, these measures exclusively protect the device owner and leave bystanders without practical ways to opt out. This normalization of passive recording undermines longstanding social norms regarding conversational privacy and places an unreasonable burden on individuals to navigate a physical landscape saturated with hidden recording technology.
